axes.model_access:
**Official position: any model LiteLLM supports can connect, and it ships its own LiteLLM gateway layer (verified).**

**Providers verified working** (selectable in the Basic settings dropdown):

- OpenHands provider
- Anthropic
- OpenAI
- Mistral AI

**How to write a Custom Model**: specify a provider prefix following LiteLLM's provider conventions;
there is also a customizable `Base URL`, through which local and self-hosted models connect.
The official docs say saving a local LLM profile first validates against the backend.

**LLM profiles**: up to 10 configurations coexist. Switch mid-session or via `/model`.
The built-in `SwitchLLMTool` also lets the agent choose dynamically.

⚠ **Two things the official docs do not give.** One: a complete provider list. Two: alignment data for "any LLM" —
i.e. whether tool calling and structured output align. Verification scope: the llm-settings page.

**This item matters especially for this object**: it is simultaneously other agents' scheduling layer.
"Codex / Claude Code run on top of it" is a special case — which models are usable is decided by that agent.

**Official LLM settings page, verbatim**: "This can be any model that is supported by litellm"
axes.runtime:
**It has four official deployment forms — the most practically valuable part of this object.** All four README Options verified.

- **Option 1 local without sandbox**: `npm install -g @openhands/agent-canvas` then
  `agent-canvas`, starts the full local stack, **requires Node.js 24+ and uv**;
  `--frontend-only` / `--backend-only` split it apart

- **Option 2 Docker sandbox**: `docker run` the official image,
  requires preparing a `PROJECTS_PATH` host directory beforehand; the agent can access projects under it

- **Option 3 per-conversation containers**: `OH_CONVERSATION_RUNTIME=docker agent-canvas`,
  each new conversation starts its own container and Agent Server — good for running multiple agents concurrently

- **Option 4 from source**: clone + `npm install` + `npm run dev`

**Entry URL**: `http://localhost:8000` (the Docker image serves `/canvas`).

**Backends can be switched remotely** — the core capability of its scheduling layer: officially the Agent Server
can run on a laptop / Mac Mini / cloud VM / OpenHands Cloud,
and the Canvas frontend switches between multiple Servers.

On Option 3 the official docs note containers mount the conversation's workspace and persisted state.
**Files and conversation history survive container replacement**.
axes.local_files:
**How much of the local file system is reachable depends on which deployment form you choose — the official docs make this variable explicit.**

- **No-sandbox form**: the agent has full file-system access; the official docs WARNING twice
- **Docker form**: access narrows to the directory mounted at `PROJECTS_PATH`
- **Per-conversation container form**: the official docs caution that **conversations sharing the same host workspace still share the same files**;
  use separate directories or worktrees to avoid conflicting edits

- **When the backend is remote** (cloud VM / Cloud backend): the agent runs in a remote workspace;
  the SDK specifies the remote working directory with `Workspace(host=..., working_dir="workspace/project")`;
  file and command operations execute server-side

**The official docs do not describe a mechanism for "auto-syncing a local repo to a remote backend"** (agent-server and runtime pages checked) —
the repo must already live remotely, or be moved by you.

**Official WARNING, verbatim**: "This runs the agent-server directly on the machine you're installing on —
**the agent will have full access to your filesystem!**"
axes.background:
**Background tasks are its most prominent strength and its biggest difference from other harness entries.**

The two biggest benefits of running agents on a cloud server: they keep running when you close the laptop,
and they are easier to trigger from third-party services like Slack, GitHub, or Datadog.

The companion is the standalone repo `OpenHands/automation`, offering two trigger modes:

- schedules
- webhook events

The official feature table lists integrable third parties: Slack, GitHub, Linear, and Notion.

**Compared with our other objects**: OpenAI Agents SDK, Deep Agents, and Codex SDK keep thread state
in their own process / own machine — gone when closed.
Only this one markets "the agent keeps running after you close the laptop".

**Official README, verbatim**: it "allows your agents to **continue running even when your laptop is shut**"

The same page names Slack, GitHub, and Datadog as easier trigger channels.

Verified `OpenHands/automation` (2026-10-01): Python, MIT, 32★, active.
axes.tools:
**It has two access lines: its own toolset + MCP; plus ACP for scheduling third-party agents.**

① **The default toolset of its own agent (CodeAct / software-agent-sdk)**, listed in the official start-conversation API example:

- `terminal`
- `file_editor`
- `task_tracker`
- `browser_tool_set` (`cli_mode` can disable browser tools)

② **MCP support verified**, with an official MCP Servers page:

- CLI uses `openhands mcp`; Canvas uses `Customize > MCP Servers`
- Transports cover http / sse / stdio
- Auth supports Bearer / API Key / OAuth
- On the SDK side, `mcp_config` (FastMCP format) injects `mcpServers`

③ Third-party agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, etc.) are scheduled via **ACP (Agent Client Protocol)**.

**⚠ Correction to the previous version of this dossier**: this object **does not go ACP-only** — MCP is equally an official capability.
axes.context:
**On context, the official docs have an explicit mechanism: the context condenser.** Evidence for this dimension is complete.

The default implementation is `LLMSummarizingCondenser` (extends `RollingCondenser`),
with parameters `max_size` / `keep_first`. Over threshold it **keeps recent messages intact and only summarizes older content**.

On the Canvas side the entry is `Settings > Condenser`;
the LLM settings page has "Enable memory condensation" and
**"Memory condenser max history size"** toggles.

The official docs also explain: with a condenser configured, exceeding the window emits a condensation-request event
instead of throwing `LLMContextWindowExceedError`. The agent summarizes old history and continues.

**⚠ Per our "state ≠ context" framing**: run history and persistence across container replacement belong to the state side.
The condenser above is the official context-side mechanism. Count them separately.

**Official SDK guide, verbatim**: the context condenser "intelligently summarizing older
parts of the conversation while preserving essential information";
over threshold it "Keeps recent messages intact", "Summarizes older content".
axes.permissions:
**This is where the official docs are most thorough — and the part that most deserves careful reading.**

**Sandbox**: the official docs give two containment measures (see local_files): the Docker sandbox and per-conversation containers.
But the official docs also explicitly offer the no-sandbox form, WARNING twice.

**Authentication uses an API key, not a user system**:

- generate a key: `openssl rand -base64 32`, assign to `LOCAL_BACKEND_API_KEY`
- in `--public` mode the **key is not baked into the frontend**; users must paste the key manually on first UI open;
  afterwards every `/api/*` request carries the `X-Session-API-Key` header

- **loopback-only binding by default** (127.0.0.1). The official rationale: keep the auto-injected session key
  from being reachable by other machines on the LAN

- when listening on `0.0.0.0` the key is no longer injected; the same API-key input UI is used instead
- the official docs advise `export` over command-line arguments for the key,
  to keep it out of `ps aux` process listings

- **exposing to the public internet carries official firewall requirements** (Cloud Firewall / AWS Security Group / GCP firewall rule)

**⚠ Multi-user and permission tiers are assigned by the official docs to Enterprise.**
The official deployment comparison table shows the Open Source tier "Users = 1";
**Multi-user RBAC and SSO/SAML exist only in Enterprise** (the OSS column reads "—").

So OSS self-hosting includes no user/role/audit system — that session key is all there is.
Multi-user tiering and auditing require Enterprise.

`docs/SELF_HOSTING.md` (verified, 286 lines) covers exactly this API-key mechanism.

**Verified**: enterprise page and deployment comparison table checked.
axes.fit:
**What it can do**:

- Put agents on your own server running 7×24
- Trigger by schedule or webhook (Slack / GitHub / Linear / Notion)
- Manage multiple agent kinds from one UI (including ACP-compatible Codex, Claude Code, Gemini)
- You need per-conversation isolated containers
- Your team deploys frontend/platform separately from the agent runtime
- Long sessions need the official condenser to control context cost

**What it is not for**:

- You just want a lightweight library to embed agents in your own Python process
  (use software-agent-sdk or OpenAI Agents SDK for that need)

- Ad-hoc single-machine use — it is a whole stack, not a library
- You need multi-user fine-grained permission tiers — the official docs assign Multi-user RBAC to Enterprise;
  OSS self-hosting has a single key only

sections.形态澄清：这不是 SDK，是平台，而且它在别人之上:
Among our three coding-base forms, it belongs to form 3, **ships a complete runtime**,
and is the **only one of those with a Web UI**.

### Three perception gaps that are easy to trip on

**① The main brand is now Agent Canvas, but the repo name hasn't changed.**

Its current positioning is a **control center**. It no longer writes itself as "a development tool".
The repo description is still the old one.

> Repo description, verbatim: "🙌 OpenHands: AI-Driven Development";
> the README's first-screen title is already Agent Canvas.

**② It runs more than OpenHands' own agent.**

The official docs list four and leave an open condition.

> README, verbatim: "OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or any ACP-compatible agent"

**It is not a competitor of the Codex SDK or Claude Agent SDK we list** — they are in a scheduler/scheduled relationship.

So the selection question is not "this or Codex" but "do you want one UI to govern
Codex / Claude Code / Gemini".

**③ The real programming entry is in another repo.**

The official three-repo division of labor, from this table:

> The official docs have a Repository boundaries table; this dossier records it verbatim.

| Repository | Responsibility | Verified (2026-10-01) |
|---|---|---|
| `OpenHands/OpenHands` | frontend control center, backend selection, local-stack orchestration | 91,593★ · MIT · TypeScript |
| `OpenHands/software-agent-sdk` | **Python SDK, Agent Server, agents, tools, conversations, workspaces, events** | 1,190★ · MIT · Python |
| `OpenHands/automation` | schedule dispatch, webhooks, run history, delivery | 32★ · MIT · Python |

> ⚠ **91,593★ is the control center's star count, not the SDK's**.
> If what you want is "an SDK embedded in your own Python process", that object is `software-agent-sdk` (1,190★),
> not this entry.
> **We did not list it separately this time** — see suggested run #1 below.
sections.档位：三档里两档是免费档，但「免费」有个硬上限:
The official pricing page verified 2026-10-01 leads to a conclusion that may differ from expectations: **there is no paid individual tier.**
(Quotes not stored per our D9 rule; see the official pricing page.)

| Tier | Deployment | Users | Daily conversations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Open Source** (free) | local | 1 | **Unlimited** |
| **SaaS Individual** (free) | cloud | 1 | **10** |
| **Enterprise** (custom, Contact Us) | SaaS or **customer's own VPC** | Unlimited | Unlimited |

**① The most critical gap: the free cloud tier caps at 10 conversations per day.**

The official comparison table's same column: Open Source = **Unlimited**, Individual = **10**, Enterprise = Unlimited.
**"Free" does not mean "unlimited"**. Two roads to unlimited: run locally, or go Enterprise.

**② Individual supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK).**

Without a key you can use the OpenHands LLM provider; generate an API key under Settings > API
for the CLI / Local Web UI / Software Agent SDK.
The official docs stress it is at cost, zero markup, pay-as-you-go.

**The official docs do not publish an actual unit-price table**; only the no-markup claim is confirmable (we also store no quotes per D9).

> Official FAQ, verbatim: all Open Source and Cloud tiers support bringing your own LLM key;
> without a key you go through the OpenHands provider, officially emphasized "**at cost, with no markup**".

**③ Individual also has a batch of things the OSS tier lacks**:
cloud access (desktop + mobile) and the Cloud API (for automation and scripts),
plus Jira and Slack integrations, Secrets, and organization support.

**④ Enterprise is actually a different thing, not "a few more users"**:

- deployable in the **customer's own VPC**
- Enterprise SAML/SSO, multi-user RBAC
- centralized team billing
- **unlimited concurrent sessions per user**
- Large Codebase SDK
- **Named Customer Engineer + shared Slack channel + priority support**

Pricing requires contacting sales.

sections.权限与安全：官方做得细，但你要选对形态:
The key design is **an API key, not a user system**.

| Mechanism | Official wording / parameter | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| key generation | `openssl rand -base64 32` → `LOCAL_BACKEND_API_KEY` | 256-bit |
| `--public` mode | key **not baked into the frontend**; users paste it on first UI open | prevents key leakage via frontend code |
| request header | every `/api/*` carries `X-Session-API-Key` | session-level auth |
| default binding | **loopback-only (127.0.0.1)** | official rationale: keep the auto-injected session key off the LAN |
| listen on all interfaces | `--host 0.0.0.0` or `OH_BIND_HOST` | then the key is not injected; same input UI instead |
| passing the key | use `export`, not command-line arguments | **keeps it out of `ps aux` listings** |
| public exposure | official firewall requirements (Cloud Firewall / AWS SG / GCP firewall rule) | |

**Multi-user and permission tiers verified (2026-10-08)**: formal RBAC / SSO sit in the Enterprise tier;
the OSS tier defaults to single user, single session key.
**Team-level use requires Enterprise, or do auth at your reverse-proxy layer.**

> `docs/SELF_HOSTING.md` (verified, 286 lines) covers only "protecting a single key";
> the official enterprise page documents RBAC / SSO.
sections.上下文维度：官方给了 condenser（2026-10-08 更新）:
This kind of object does persistence well — run history, history surviving container replacement.
**Handling long conversation context also has an official mechanism**. It is on the SDK side: the context condenser.

Per our claim "**state ≠ context**":

- **state** ✅ official evidence (schedule/webhook triggers, run history, history preserved across container replacement)
- **context** ✅ official mechanism (condenser); real compression effect awaits testing

**Persistence ≠ context management** — still two things; but this object can now deliver the latter.

> The official sdk/guides page gives `LLMSummarizingCondenser` / `RollingCondenser`.

sections.核验说明:
Basis for `confidence: partial`:

**Why not verified**: no axis is missing. All eight axes were verified to official mechanisms this round (the `context` side has the official
condenser, see axes.context). It stays partial because items remain that **the official docs genuinely don't state, or that need testing**:

- end-to-end effect of context compression
- the local→remote workspace sync mechanism (not stated officially)
- the positioning boundary between ACP and MCP
- the concrete contents of the Enterprise tier (official docs only say Custom pricing / Contact Us)

Per the v3 rule "say unknown when unknown", it stays partial.

**Verified (this part is solid)**:

- Repository existence and star count (91,593 · rolling verification 2026-10-23), license (MIT, via license API)
- Last push (2026-10-22, still active), latest release **v1.31.0** (releases @ 2026-10-22)
- Full README nine sections (positioning, four-item feature table, Quickstart's four Options, Architecture and
  Repository boundaries table, More documentation)

- Security-mechanism highlights of the 286-line `docs/SELF_HOSTING.md`
- Repo top-level directory structure (`helm/`, `vercel.json`, `electron-builder.config.mjs`,
  `.openhands/`, `docker/`, etc.)

- Metadata of the `software-agent-sdk` and `automation` repos

> `software-agent-sdk` (1,190★ · MIT · Python), `automation` (32★ · MIT · Python).

**Not verified**:

- Measured effect of conversation-context compression
- The local→remote workspace sync mechanism (not stated officially)
- The API shape of `software-agent-sdk`
- The full configuration format of LLM profiles (the official page has it; details not entered item by item)

**Added this round (2026-10-01)**: the official pricing page's three tiers verified —
Open Source and Cloud Individual both free tiers, Enterprise custom;
**Individual's 10-conversation daily cap** (versus Open Source's Unlimited);
Individual supports BYOK; without a key the OpenHands provider applies, officially **at cost, no markup**;
Enterprise can deploy in the customer's own VPC, with SAML/SSO, RBAC, unlimited per-user concurrency.
Enterprise tier specifics remain unverified (and we store no quote numbers per D9).

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested runs** (tailored to this object's form):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | Can `software-agent-sdk` alone (no Canvas) run a minimal agent | decides whether you need the whole stack at all |
| 2 | Condenser compression effect and cost change on long (multi-day) tasks | mechanism known (LLMSummarizingCondenser); compression ratio needs testing |
| 3 | **Real isolation strength of per-conversation containers** (the shared-host-workspace caveat needs testing) | the official docs already flag the conflict risk |
| 4 | In Docker form, can the agent escape `PROJECTS_PATH` to reach other host paths | sandbox validity is a selection precondition |
| 5 | Real onboarding cost of attaching Claude Code / Codex as ACP agents | its most unique selling point; worth it depends on this |
| 6 | Idempotency and duplicate-trigger handling of webhook triggers | schedules/webhooks are its flagship scenario |
unknowns:
- Provider capability alignment of "any LLM" (list verified: verbatim "any model that is supported by litellm")
- End-to-end effect of conversation-context compression (official condenser exists; compression ratio awaits testing)
- Multi-user arrangements in the OSS tier (formal RBAC / SSO in Enterprise; OSS defaults to single user)
- The positioning difference between ACP and MCP (both usable; the boundary is not systematically compared officially)
- **The concrete contents of the Enterprise tier** (official docs only mark Custom pricing / Contact Us; quotes not recorded per D9)
- Behavior beyond Individual's daily 10 conversations (disabled / upgrade prompt / other — not written on the official page)
- The sync mechanism for local codebases when the backend is deployed remotely
- The API shape and independent versioning cadence of `software-agent-sdk`
- Resource usage and stability of per-conversation containers under concurrency stress
related: **A scheduling relationship, not a competitive one**: the README states plainly that Agent Canvas can run Codex. This dossier is about "who schedules for you"; codex-sdk is about "what gets scheduled".
Same as above: Claude Code is also one of the agents it declares it can schedule.
Both in the batteries-included tier, but deepagents is a library while OpenHands is a whole stack with a Web UI.
If what you want is "define flows in code" rather than "schedule agents through a UI", an orchestration framework is the matching layer.
